blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

A graph is nodes connected by edges. Grids, courses with prerequisites, friend networks, word transformations and maps are all graphs in disguise. The skill is (1) **modelling** the problem as nodes and edges, and (2) picking the right traversal.

| Need | Tool | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Visit everything reachable, count components | DFS or BFS with a `visited` set | O(V + E) |
| Shortest path in an **unweighted** graph (fewest moves) | BFS | First time you reach a node is the shortest |
| Order tasks with prerequisites, detect a cycle | Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm with in-degrees, or DFS) | Only for directed graphs |
| "Are these two connected?", merge groups, find a redundant edge | Union-Find (disjoint set) | Nearly O(1) per operation |
| Shortest path with weights | Dijkstra | See *Advanced Graphs* |

"number of islands or regions", "connected", "prerequisite", "course schedule", "shortest number of steps", "minimum moves", "clone", "valid tree". A grid is a graph where each cell has up to four neighbours.
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: How a graph is stored decides the code: an **adjacency list** (`List<List<Integer>>` or `Map<Integer, List<Integer>>`) takes O(V + E) space and suits sparse graphs, an **adjacency matrix** takes O(V²) and suits dense graphs and quick edge checks, and a grid needs no extra structure: the neighbours are computed from the coordinates.

blocks.title: GraphTemplates.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** In `orangesRotting`, **multi-source BFS** starts with every rotten orange in the queue, so all of them spread in parallel. `size` is read before the level loop so that one pass equals one minute. `UnionFind.union` returning a boolean is what turns "redundant connection" and "graph valid tree" into one-liners.

- **Marking visited too late.** Mark a node when you *enqueue* it (BFS), not when you dequeue it, or it can be queued many times.
- **Directed versus undirected.** Add the edge in both directions for undirected graphs, and remember that "parent" must be ignored when detecting cycles with DFS.
- **Cycle detection in directed graphs** needs three states (unvisited, in progress, done) in DFS, or Kahn's algorithm; a plain `visited` set gives false positives.
- **Deep recursion.** DFS on a 1000 x 1000 grid can overflow the Java stack: use BFS or an explicit stack.
- **Modifying the input grid** is fine in interviews if you say so; otherwise use a separate `boolean[][]`.
BFS. It explores in order of distance, so the first time it reaches the target is via a shortest path (in an unweighted graph). DFS finds *a* path, not necessarily the shortest one.
blocks.title: Interview angle: BFS or DFS for shortest path in a maze?
Key points
blocks.text:
- Model the problem: what are the nodes, what are the edges?
- DFS or BFS with a visited set is O(V + E); BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs
- Multi-source BFS starts with all sources in the queue
- Kahn's algorithm orders prerequisites and detects cycles by counting taken nodes
- Union-Find answers connectivity and finds the edge that closes a cycle
- Mark visited when enqueuing; beware recursion depth on large grids

blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Graphs** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

blocks.title: Premium problems
blocks.text: Problems marked LeetCode Premium need a paid LeetCode account. If you do not have one, skip them: the free problems of the topic teach the same ideas.

items.question: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
items.answer: Run Kahn's algorithm: if fewer than n nodes can be taken (some never reach in-degree 0), a cycle exists. Or use DFS with three states and report a cycle when you reach a node that is still in progress.

items.question: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
items.answer: It visits nodes in non-decreasing order of distance from the source, so the first time a node is reached it is by a path with the fewest edges.

items.question: What does Union-Find give you that DFS does not?
items.answer: Fast incremental connectivity: after each new edge you can ask whether two nodes are already connected in nearly O(1), without re-traversing the graph. That suits problems where edges arrive one by one.
